title: The Golden Bricks
summary: A nobleman builds a house with bricks covered in gold leaf. Birbal shows him where real golden monuments are built.
full_text:
A vain and wealthy merchant of Agra named Seth Manikchand spent ten thousand gold coins building a luxurious pleasure pavilion with walls faced in bricks covered with shimmering gold leaf. He invited Emperor Akbar and the court to admire his masterpiece:

'Behold, Your Majesty! My golden mansion shall stand for centuries, proving my immense wealth to future generations!'

Akbar looked at the shining walls, but Birbal looked at the crumbling, roofless public orphanage situated right across the dusty street, where barefoot children shivered in the cold.

Birbal stepped forward and said: 'Seth Manikchand, your golden bricks are indeed bright. But tell me—what happens when the rains fall, and looters come with chisels in the night?'

'I have twenty armed guards to protect my walls!' the merchant boasted.

Birbal sighed: 'Then you are a prisoner of your own bricks! Look across the street at those fifty freezing orphan children.

'If you had used that gold to rebuild their roof, feed their hungry bellies, and teach them trades, you would have built fifty living, breathing golden monuments in the hearts of human beings! Living monuments pray for your soul, preserve your honor, and enter heaven before you. But dead bricks of gold breed only envy, theft, and vanity.'

The merchant looked at the shivering orphans, then at his cold, gilded walls. The mirror of truth shattered his vanity.

Weeping with remorse, Manikchand pledged half his fortune to rebuild the orphanage and provide food for the poor. Akbar praised Birbal for reminding everyone that the only true wealth is kindness.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Golden Bricks"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
